taciturn

TAS-ih-turn · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Taciturn is reserved or uncommunicative; habitually saying very little.

The librarian's taciturn nod was the closest thing to a greeting most visitors ever got.

Example

The taciturn shopkeeper rang up each purchase without a single word of small talk, nodding once at the door as customers left.

Saying almost nothing, even in situations where a little chat would be normal, is exactly the quiet reserve taciturn describes.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

tight-lipped: Tight-lipped describes someone refusing to talk about one particular subject -- a coach staying tight-lipped about the starting lineup. Taciturn is broader and more settled: a taciturn person says little about everything, in every setting, as a matter of temperament, not because one topic is off-limits.

laconic: Laconic describes a style of speaking that uses the fewest words possible -- brief replies that still say everything needed. Taciturn describes the person rather than the style: a settled disposition to say little at all. A laconic answer is compact and complete; a taciturn person barely answers.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

talkative: fond of talking a great deal

outgoing: socially confident and eager to engage

Where it sits · how firmly words are held back — reserved → taciturn → reticent

reserved vs. taciturn: Reserved is milder than taciturn: a reserved person is simply slow to open up and often chats freely once comfortable, while a taciturn one stays sparing with words day after day, even among old friends.

reticent vs. taciturn: Reticent is stronger than taciturn: a taciturn person simply says little out of habit, while a reticent one goes further, deliberately refusing to reveal things -- not even discussing the diagnosis with close family.

Build the Word

The pieces

root — tacit- (tacere)

root — tacit- (tacere): to be silent (Latin)

suffix — -urn

suffix — -urn: tending to (Latin -urnus) (Latin)

Put it together

Put it together: Taciturn comes from Latin tacere, 'to be silent,' plus the ending -urn, 'tending to' (Latin -urnus, the same ending hiding in nocturne) -- so a taciturn person tends toward silence by nature, saying little even when there is a chance to speak.

Use the root in a new word: tacit

Use the root in a new word: tacit: There was a tacit understanding among the roommates that whoever cooked dinner didn't have to do the dishes.

Word Choice

Taciturn describes a person's general, everyday habit of speaking little -- contrast it with cagey, taught later in this unit, which describes someone deliberately withholding specific information when pressed, and brusque, which is about a blunt tone rather than overall silence.
